left.head: 9pm. Pyjamas on. The TV comes back on.

right.tag: The same evening, side by side
right.head: Same child. Same clock. One difference.

left.head: Her eyes lock on. That is a reflex.
left.body: Cuts and sound changes pull a young child's attention automatically. Not a choice.

right.head: She came down and put the TV on again.
right.body: She is six. What do I do?

left.head: Each clip is a new guess at what comes next.
left.body: Dopamine drives the wanting, not the pleasure. Up next never offers her the end.

right.head: Tonight is not the night to fight it.
right.body: Sit with her for the last five minutes. Then off at the end of this one, and up together.
right.src: Rails: no blame, no battle at bedtime

left.head: She cannot stop by herself yet.
left.body: Stopping needs the front of the brain, which is years from ready at six. The pull wins.

right.head: The ending is built in.
right.body: Children were less upset when screen time was routine, and when the technology ended it rather than a parent.

left.head: Evening light hits a child's melatonin hard.
left.body: Far harder than an adult's. Even dim room light cut preschoolers' melatonin by about three quarters.

right.head: Tomorrow, set the shape of the evening early.
right.body: Screen off at half past seven, then a story with you. A nightly routine means earlier, longer sleep.

left.head: A late, irregular bedtime shows up the next day.
left.body: Shorter fuse, less joy, poorer attention. In 10,000 UK children, regular bedtimes meant better behaviour at seven.

right.head: Did it work? Tell DiGi.
right.body: Your answer feeds the next one. Across families only counts travel, never your words.

beats.head: Start free. Three questions, no sign up.
beats.body: Find your child's stage, then ask DiGi your own 9pm question.
